Part 1

What evapotranspiration is

Why ET matters, what drives evaporation, and the role of vapor pressure deficit

Why do we care about evapotranspiration?

Key idea

Evapotranspiration is a major component of the water cycle: over land it returns more than 60% of precipitation to the air.

Evapotranspiration (ET) is the combined name for evaporation and transpiration.

Read the figure

  • Over land, precipitation is 115 and ET is 75: ET returns about 65% (the red “> 60%” arrow)
  • ET (75) is about 15% of all water vapor entering the atmosphere (75 of 75 + 431)

Why it matters

ET recycles water vapor over the continents. Without it, far less precipitation would fall on land.

Evaporation

Key idea

Evaporation moves water from the liquid phase to the gas phase, and it requires energy, mainly from the sun.

Where does it happen?

Water, soil and canopy

What does it need?

  • A supply of water
  • A receiving atmosphere that can take the vapor

Energy

The energy required is the latent heat of vaporization (Lecture 4b).

Evapotranspiration is the sum of evaporation from the land surface plus transpiration from plants.

What factors affect evaporation?

Key idea

Evaporation needs energy, a dry, moving atmosphere, and a supply of water.

Factors affecting evaporation

  • Water temperature and air temperature
  • Humidity
  • Energy source (solar radiation)
  • Wind, which carries vapor away from the surface
  • Water supply, especially through soil or plant tissues

Evaporation occurs from any wet surface

Lakes, ponds and rivers; wet pavement, cars and skin; wet leaves (interception evaporation); wet ground (soil evaporation); open leaf pores (transpiration)

Note: steam is not water vapor. It is the visible mist formed when invisible hot vapor mixes with cooler air.

What factors affect transpiration?

Key idea

The same atmospheric factors that drive evaporation also control how fast plants transpire, plus soil moisture and plant type.

Temperature

Rates rise with temperature, especially in the growing season. Warmth opens the stomata (leaf pores); cold closes them.

Relative humidity

As humidity around the plant rises, transpiration falls. Water evaporates more easily into drier air.

Wind and air movement

Wind replaces the saturated air next to the leaf with drier air, raising the rate.

Soil moisture

When moisture is lacking, plants can senesce (age early, losing leaves) and transpire less.

Type of plant

Plants transpire at different rates. Cacti and succulents in arid regions conserve water by transpiring less.

We usually just call it ET

Key idea

ET = E + T: evaporation from wet surfaces plus transpiration through plants.

  • (E) Evaporation: intercepted water, open water, soil water
  • (T) Transpiration: water transpired by plants, along the path

soil water → roots → xylem → leaves → stomata

Evapotranspiration is not…

  • Sublimation: solid directly to gas, skipping the liquid state
  • Condensation: water vapor becoming liquid, the reverse of evaporation

Read the figure

The phase changes of matter. ET is only the liquid → gas arrow (evaporation).

How does ET work?

Key idea

ET converts liquid water to vapor and transfers it to the atmosphere. It is driven by the vapor pressure deficit (VPD).

VPD = eₛ (saturation) − eₐ (air)

Read the left figure

Molecules leave the wet surface (Tₛ) and mix into the air above (Tₐ). Transfer continues as long as the air is not saturated.

Read the right figure

Point B is the saturation vapor pressure at 20 °C; point A is the actual vapor pressure at 43% RH. The gap between them is the VPD.

Bigger VPD → drier air → faster ET.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q1 Using the global water cycle figure, what fraction of land precipitation returns to the air as ET?

75 / 115 ≈ 65%, which is the “> 60%” shown on the figure.

Q2 Why does wind increase evaporation and transpiration?

Wind replaces the saturated air next to the surface or leaf with drier air, keeping the vapor pressure deficit high.

Q3 Is sublimation part of ET? Explain.

No. ET is liquid water becoming vapor (evaporation and transpiration). Sublimation goes from solid directly to gas.

Part 2

Potential, actual and reference ET

The rate the atmosphere could take versus the rate that really happens

Potential vs. actual evaporation

Key idea

Potential ET assumes unlimited water. Actual ET is what really happens with the water that is available.

  • PE: evaporation rate given an unrestricted supply of water
  • AE: evaporation rate given a restricted supply (the amount that actually occurs)
  • Reference ET: usually calculated for a well-watered grass surface

Factors affecting AE

Precipitation, local heat budget, soil moisture availability, water table

Read the graphs

Monthly precipitation (■), potential ET (○) and actual ET (△). In summer, PET exceeds precipitation, so AE falls below PET: there is not enough water to meet the demand.

Reference evapotranspiration (ET₀)

Key idea

ET₀ is the ET rate over a well-watered, short green grass-like crop: the “drying power of a climate.”

Also related to crop ET.

  • Because the surface is fixed, ET₀ depends only on atmospheric conditions
  • Important for improved agricultural water management

Read the figure

Reference ET (red) follows the weather through the season. Crop ET (blue) starts low while the crop is small, matches or exceeds ET₀ at full canopy, then falls as the crop matures.

Try it

OpenET is a free tool for estimating crop ET from satellite data.

Definitions to remember

Key idea

Keep these six terms straight; the rest of the lecture uses all of them.

  • Evaporation: water changes from liquid to vapor and leaves a water or land surface
  • Transpiration: water moves through plants and evaporates through leaf stomata
  • Evapotranspiration: the combined processes of evaporation (water, soil, leaf surfaces) and transpiration (leaf interior)
  • Potential evapotranspiration (PET): water evaporated per unit area and time from an idealized free water surface, given current atmospheric conditions
  • Reference ET (ET₀): ET from a specific reference crop under well-watered conditions
  • Actual ET (ETₐ): ET under the existing meteorological, soil, cover and water-availability conditions

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q4 In a dry summer month, PET is 140 mm but actual ET is only 50 mm. Explain the difference.

PET assumes unlimited water. Actual ET is limited by the water available (precipitation, soil moisture), so it falls well below PET in a dry month.

Q5 Why does reference ET₀ depend only on the weather?

The surface is fixed: a well-watered, short grass crop. With the surface and water supply held constant, only atmospheric conditions change it.

Part 3

Where ET happens

Evaporation from open water, soil and canopies, and transpiration from plants

Evaporation from open water

  1. Open water
  2. Soil
  3. Canopy
  4. Transpiration
Key idea

Open water is the simplest form of ET: water lost from lakes and reservoirs, often estimated with an evaporation pan.

  • Often estimated from the loss in a National Weather Service Class A pan
  • The pan should have straight sides and sit on an open platform

Pan evaporation ≈ PET

It is the maximum rate possible under the weather: water is unlimited, energy is abundant, and vapor escapes freely.

PET = (change in pan water depth) × (pan coefficient)

Read the map

Pan evaporation ranges from about 30 in/yr in Seattle to over 100 in/yr in West Texas and Imperial Valley, CA. Pans are commonly used for lakes, ponds and reservoirs.

Evaporation from soil

  1. Open water
  2. Soil
  3. Canopy
  4. Transpiration
Key idea

Soil evaporation is fast while the surface is wet, then drops sharply as the soil dries. (More in Chapter 6.)

Controlled by

  • Available energy
  • The soil's ability to wick water up to near the surface
  • Diffusion of water vapor out of soil surface pores

Read the graph

  • Wet soil: water is easy to reach at the surface → fast, steady evaporation
  • Drying soil: water must be wicked up from deeper, and less wet surface area remains → evaporation slows

Watch out

If it goes on too long without freshwater flushing, soil evaporation causes salinization.

Evaporation from the canopy

  1. Open water
  2. Soil
  3. Canopy
  4. Transpiration
Key idea

Interception is precipitation retained by the vegetation canopy. It is the dominant evaporative loss in many forests.

Interception

  • Retains 10% – 50% of gross annual rainfall
  • Reduces rainfall intensity and erosivity
  • Can it be negative? Yes: fog or cloud interception and condensation can add water

Net precipitation (throughfall)

The amount of precipitation that actually reaches the ground.

Read the figure

Precipitation → canopy interception → throughfall and stemflow → forest floor interception → infiltration.

Transpiration

  1. Open water
  2. Soil
  3. Canopy
  4. Transpiration
Key idea

Transpiration is how water vapor escapes from living plants into the atmosphere, mostly through leaf stomata.

  • Includes water transpired through leaf stomata
  • Also includes intercepted water that has re-evaporated

Hard to measure

Transpiration is very difficult to measure on its own, so it is usually lumped in with evaporation as ET.

Factors affecting transpiration

Plant type, stage of growth, season, time of day, soil properties and meteorological factors.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q6 Why does evaporation from a bare soil slow down a few days after rain?

The surface dries: water must be wicked up from deeper layers and less wet surface area is left, so the rate drops.

Q7 A forest receives 1,000 mm of rain a year and the canopy intercepts 25%. How much is net precipitation (throughfall plus stemflow)?

1,000 × 0.75 = 750 mm reaches the ground; 250 mm is intercepted and evaporates.

Q8 Why is transpiration usually reported together with evaporation as ET?

Transpiration is very difficult to measure separately, so it is lumped with evaporation.

Part 4

Measuring evaporation

Micrometeorological methods, evaporation pans and lysimeters

Why estimate evapotranspiration?

Key idea

ET matters for climate, crops, reservoirs and runoff models, but it is very difficult to estimate.

Why we need it

  • Climate change
  • ET supports plant growth; irrigation requires knowledge of transpiration
  • Evaporation loss from reservoirs, and other human uses
  • Potential errors in rainfall–runoff models

How it is estimated

Usually with models based on water balances, temperature index, energy balances, mass transfer, or a combination approach.

Micrometeorological measurements of evaporation

Key idea

Three methods measure vapor and energy above the surface to find actual evaporation.

Eddy fluctuation (eddy correlation)

  • Measures the upward movement of water vapor above a surface
  • Needs detailed instruments, such as a hot-wire anemometer
  • Very short time scales (high-frequency readings)
  • Small surface
  • No assumed values of atmospheric parameters

Aerodynamic profile

  • Vapor transport away from the surface as a function of the humidity gradient and wind speed
  • Needs the change in temperature and humidity with height
  • Assumes the atmosphere is neutral and stable

Bowen ratio

B = H / λE

  • Ratio of sensible to latent heat
  • No assumptions about air temperature and humidity
  • No wind data needed
  • Best with 30-minute averages

Instruments for the Bowen ratio and eddy covariance methods

Key idea

Bowen ratio stations measure gradients at two heights; eddy covariance measures fast fluctuations at one point.

Aerodynamic profile (left)

Net radiation Rₙ enters from above; air flow carries away the evaporated water E.

Bowen ratio station (right, A)

Net radiometer, anemometer, upper and lower air temperature and humidity probes, plus soil moisture, soil temperature and soil heat flux sensors.

Eddy covariance station (right, B)

A 3-D sonic anemometer, a fine-wire thermocouple and a krypton hygrometer sample wind, temperature and humidity many times per second.

Indirect measurement: potential ET

Key idea

PET is a theoretical ET rate when all surfaces have unlimited water. Treat it as an index.

Assumptions

  • Uniform vegetation height and completely shaded ground
  • Unlimited water supply

Background

It began in studies of irrigated crops, to estimate their consumptive use.

PET is estimated with

  • Evaporation pans and crop coefficients
  • Numerical models (Part 5)

Read the figure

Climate (radiation, temperature, wind, humidity) + a well-watered surface of undefined land cover = PET.

Evaporation pan method

Key idea

A pan measures open-water evaporation (E₀) from the daily drop in its water level, corrected for rain.

How it works

  • Water depth is read with a high-precision micrometer, a hook gauge, in a stilling well
  • A precipitation gauge sits directly next to the pan

E = P − ΔS

where ΔS is the change in pan water depth (negative when the level falls).

Issues

  • Edge effect: warm air takes up more vapor at the edge than over the middle of a large water body
  • Pan coefficient: the pan's sides and shallow water absorb radiation and warm faster than a lake. The annual pan coefficient in the U.S. is about 0.7

Lysimeters: measuring actual ET

Key idea

A lysimeter is a soil tank whose water balance gives actual evapotranspiration.

E = P − Q − ΔS

(precipitation in, drainage Q out, ΔS the change in soil water storage)

Weighing lysimeter

Weighs the tank (for example with a hydraulic pressure gauge) alongside a precipitation gauge, so ΔS is measured directly.

Percolation gauge

Used when there is no weighing instrument; it assumes no change in soil moisture.

Issues

  • The same edge effect as the pan
  • Impossible to perfectly recreate the surrounding land
  • Reasonable only over long periods, such as a year

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q9 What does the Bowen ratio compare, and what data does it not need?

Sensible heat to latent heat (B = H / λE). It does not need wind data.

Q10 A Class A pan loses 8 mm of water in a day with no rain. Using a pan coefficient of 0.7, estimate lake evaporation.

8 × 0.7 = 5.6 mm/day.

Q11 Over a year, a lysimeter receives 900 mm of precipitation, drains 200 mm, and its storage is unchanged. What is the actual ET?

E = P − Q − ΔS = 900 − 200 − 0 = 700 mm.

Part 5

Models to estimate ET

Thornthwaite, Penman and Penman–Monteith

Models to estimate potential ET

Key idea

Two classic PET models: Thornthwaite (temperature-based) and Penman (energy plus mass transfer).

C. W. Thornthwaite (1899–1963)

American geographer. His method needs only temperature and day length.

Howard Penman (1909–1984)

British meteorologist. His method combines radiation and vapor transport, so it needs much more data.

The Thornthwaite method

Key idea

Thornthwaite estimates monthly PET from mean temperature and day length alone.

Data needs

Mean temperature for each of the 12 months (Tₐ), and average day length (L)

Suitable for

Monthly PET where little data is available; works best in moderate climates (not too dry or humid)

Terms

  • N: days in the month
  • I: heat index, summed over the 12 monthly temperatures
  • α: an exponent calculated from I

With the coefficient 16 the result is in mm per month (the original slide said cm).

The Penman method

Key idea

Penman combines a radiation term and a mass-transfer term: more physically based, but it needs lots of data.

Read the equation

  • ΔRₙ: radiation term (Δ = slope of the saturation vapor pressure curve, Rₙ = net radiation)
  • γ(eₛ − eₐ): mass-transfer term (γ = psychrometric constant, eₛ − eₐ = vapor pressure deficit)
  • λ: latent heat of vaporization

Trade-off

  • Advantage: more physically based
  • Disadvantage: requires lots of data

Gives PET for reference vegetation using full climate data.

From Penman to Penman–Monteith

Key idea

Penman gives evaporation only. Penman–Monteith adds conductances so it covers canopy evaporation and transpiration.

Penman: just evaporation

Radiation plus mass transfer from a wet surface.

Penman–Monteith: evaporation from the canopy and transpiration

Adds three new pieces:

  • G: ground heat flux
  • ρₐcₐ: density and specific heat of air
  • C_atm / C_canopy: atmospheric and canopy conductances

So what is all the extra stuff? The next slides explain the conductances.

Penman–Monteith: conductance and resistance

Key idea

A conductance is how easily vapor moves from the leaf to the air; it is the inverse of a resistance.

Read the diagram

Vapor leaving the leaf meets two resistances in series:

  • rₛ, surface resistance: through the stomata, cuticle and soil
  • rₐ, aerodynamic resistance: from the evaporating surface up to a reference level in the air

In the equation

  • C_atm = 1 / rₐ, the atmospheric conductance
  • C_canopy = 1 / rₛ, the canopy conductance

Low conductance (high resistance) means less ET for the same weather.

Atmospheric conductance (C_atm)

Key idea

C_atm comes from an assumed smooth logarithmic wind profile above the surface.

Terms

  • v_m: wind velocity
  • k: von Kármán constant = 0.41
  • z_m: measurement height, often 2 m
  • z_d: zero-plane displacement height = (2/3) h, for canopy height h
  • z_0M: roughness length for momentum = 0.123 h
  • z_0H: roughness length for heat = 0.1 z_0M

Taller, rougher canopies and stronger wind → higher C_atm.

Canopy conductance (C_can)

Key idea

Canopy conductance is built from empirical environmental feedback functions that scale a maximum leaf conductance.

Terms

  • fₛ: fraction of leaves that are shaded
  • LAI: leaf area index
  • C∗_leaf: maximum leaf conductance
  • f_K(K_in): solar radiation
  • f_ρ(Δρ_v): vapor density deficit
  • f_T(Tₐ): air temperature
  • f_θ(Δθ): soil moisture deficit

Each function is between 0 and 1, so any stress (dry soil, low light, dry air) reduces canopy conductance.

Transpiration vs. evaporation in Penman–Monteith

Key idea

The main difference is resistance from the stomata, the canopy conductance term.

Think it through

For evaporation from a wet surface (open water, a wet canopy), there are no stomata in the way: canopy resistance is near zero, and the equation behaves like Penman.

For transpiration, water must pass through the stomata. That resistance appears in the circled term, C_atm / C_canopy.

Good and bad uses of the Penman–Monteith method

Key idea

Penman–Monteith is only as good as the canopy conductance you can give it.

Good uses

Very good for estimating actual ET if you:

  • have meteorological data, and
  • have canopy surface resistance measurements or estimates, or can calibrate canopy conductance

Bad uses

If you don't have reasonable parameters available to calculate canopy conductance.

Putting the three models side by side

Thornthwaite: monthly PET from temperature and day length; little data. Penman: PET from radiation + mass transfer; lots of data. Penman–Monteith: actual ET including transpiration; also needs canopy conductance.

Check your understanding

Answer in your own words first, then open the answer to check.

Q12 You have only monthly mean temperatures for a remote basin. Which PET model can you use, and what is its main limitation?

Thornthwaite. It is temperature-based, so it ignores radiation, humidity and wind, and works best in moderate climates.

Q13 What does Penman–Monteith add to the Penman equation, and why?

Conductances (atmospheric and canopy), plus ground heat flux and air properties, so it can include transpiration through stomata, not just evaporation.

Q14 What is the relationship between conductance and resistance, and what happens to ET when stomata close?

Conductance = 1 / resistance. Closing stomata raises resistance and lowers canopy conductance, so ET falls.
